925.title: Kierkegaard
925.hook: a Danish philosopher: faith is a leap, and life is lived forward but understood backward
925.howItsDone: Christian thinkers, preachers and students read Kierkegaard on faith as a personal risk, especially Fear and Trembling and its reading of Abraham.

segments.voice: Yesterday: The Way of a Pilgrim, and the Jesus Prayer that kept going like breath. Your line was pray without ceasing.

Hindsight is a strange gift. Looking back, a breakup can make sense, or a job that fell through, or a dreaded move that turned out to be where everything started. At the time, there is only the edge, and not knowing. A Danish writer in Copenhagen put that into one of his journals, and readers still quote it: life can only be understood backward, but it has to be lived forward. He was a philosopher, a sharp critic of comfortable churchgoing, and a Christian who thought real faith asks for everything. Today: Kierkegaard.

Søren Kierkegaard wrote much of his work under made-up names, each a different voice arguing a different view, so readers would have to think for themselves. The journal line is his own, paraphrased here: philosophers are right that life must be understood backward, but they forget the other half. It must be lived forward, and you never get to stand still long enough to understand it all before the next step. That's where faith comes in. In Fear and Trembling, written under the name Johannes de silentio, John of silence, he circles one story: Abraham, called to take his son Isaac up Mount Moriah. The book's author says he can admire Abraham, but cannot understand him. Faith, here, goes where the argument can't follow. Hebrews sums up Abraham's faith from its first step, in the King James Bible: "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went." For Kierkegaard, that is faith: not a conclusion at the end of an argument, but a step taken before you can see where it leads. He wrote about it as a leap, and some readers sum up his whole idea as the leap of faith. He had little patience for a Christianity that cost nothing; in comfortable Denmark, he thought, it was too easy to be a Christian by birth certificate. Real faith, he argued, is a personal, lived risk, made by one person standing before God. His challenge to readers: admire Abraham from a safe distance, or step out yourself, not knowing whither you go.
screen: `FAITH AS A LEAP, NOT A CONCLUSION.`

926.title: Father Zosima
926.hook: Dostoevsky's holy elder teaches that each of us is responsible for all
926.howItsDone: Some readers, Orthodox and others, turn to Zosima's teachings in The Brothers Karamazov as a picture of the Russian elder tradition, sometimes alongside Paul's call to bear one another's burdens.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kierkegaard, and a life understood backward but lived forward. Your line was lived forward.

A young army officer comes home in a rage the night before a duel. His orderly, a servant named Afanasy, does something small that annoys him, and the officer hits him in the face, hard, twice. Afanasy just stands there and takes it. In the morning the officer wakes early and steps to the window. The sun is coming up over the garden, the birds are singing, and something cuts into him like a knife. He remembers Afanasy standing there, arms at his sides, not even daring to lift a hand. This story is told inside a novel by the Russian writer Dostoevsky, by an old monk looking back on his own youth. Today: Father Zosima.

Father Zosima is a character in The Brothers Karamazov, an elder in a Russian monastery, sought out by townspeople for counsel. He isn't a historical saint; he's Dostoevsky's picture of one. At the heart of his teaching is a thought he first heard from his older brother, Markel, who was dying young. Markel tells their mother that each of us is guilty before everyone, for everyone and everything, and that he is the most guilty of all. The grown-ups think it's the illness talking. Years later, at that window, the young officer finally understands. He runs to Afanasy, bows to the ground, and asks his forgiveness. Then he goes to the duel, lets his opponent fire first, throws his own pistol away, and asks forgiveness of him too. His fellow officers are scandalized. He leaves the army, and in time becomes a monk. As an old man, Zosima teaches it plainly, paraphrased: each of us is responsible for all, for everyone and everything. He doesn't mean that each person caused every wrong. He means no one can say a suffering is none of their business. Every word, look and act goes out into the world and touches others. So for Zosima, the way out of blame and despair is to take on a share of the weight. Paul wrote something close, in the King James Bible: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Zosima goes one step further: not only helping carry the burden, but treating it as partly your own.
screen: `A BOW, AND A PISTOL THROWN AWAY.`

927.title: Lead, kindly light
927.hook: John Henry Newman, stuck on a windless sea, writes a poem that asks for one step at a time
927.howItsDone: Newman's poem is sung as the hymn Lead, Kindly Light in some English-speaking churches, and Christians in hard seasons sometimes pray its lines when they can't see what comes next.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Father Zosima, who taught that each of us answers for everyone. Your line was responsible for all.

No wind. A sailing boat sits on flat water between Corsica and Sardinia, going nowhere. On board is an English clergyman named John Henry Newman, weak from a fever he caught in Sicily, aching to get home, and unable to move. You can't argue with a calm sea, and you can't row a sailing boat home. You can only wait. So, by the story Newman himself told, he writes a short poem. It's honest about the dark, and it asks for surprisingly little. Later it became a hymn. Today's word is its first word, and it's a request.
screen: `A SICK MAN WANTS TO GO HOME.`

segments.voice: The poem opens: "Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom, Lead Thou me on!" He doesn't ask for the wind, or a map. Then the line the poem leans on: "Keep Thou my feet; I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me." Turn it one way, and it's a confession, from the next verse: "I loved to choose and see my path; but now Lead Thou me on!" A man who liked to plan, stuck on a sea that won't take orders. Turn it another way, and it's very old. Newman called the poem The Pillar of the Cloud, pointing back to Exodus, where the King James Bible says "the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light." Israel in the wilderness never saw the whole route either; they followed the cloud. Turn it a third way, and it sounds like a psalm: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet." A lamp at night lights the ground right in front of you, and almost nothing beyond. Enough to walk. And a fourth way: his own life. The path Newman couldn't see took him somewhere he never planned. Years later he left the Church of England and became a Catholic, which cost him friends, and the Catholic Church later named him a saint. Anglicans and Catholics both claim parts of his story. The poem stays the same: one step, then the next.
screen: `I LOVED TO CHOOSE AND SEE MY PATH.`
then, large: `ONE STEP ENOUGH FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Set down the worries about how things turn out, next month, next year, the end of the road, one at a time, like heavy bags: the distant scene. Then look only at the next hour and what it asks, maybe something small: a glass of water, a reply, a rest. If you pray, borrow Newman's words, lead Thou me on; if not, let that small thing be enough.

928.title: Elizabeth Fry
928.hook: a Quaker woman walks into the women's side of Newgate prison, sits down, and reads
928.howItsDone: In some churches, prison ministry teams visit people in jail, lead Bible studies, write letters and support families, often pointing to Matthew 25 as the reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Newman on a windless sea, asking to be led, not to see the distant scene. Your line was one step enough.

The door to the women's side of Newgate prison in London opens, and a woman in plain Quaker clothes steps through. Inside, women awaiting trial and women already sentenced are crowded together, some with their children, short of clothes and short of hope. The story told about that first visit is that the keepers warned her it wasn't safe, and that she went in anyway. She doesn't preach at anyone. She sits down. She asks about the children. Her name is Elizabeth Fry, a wife, a mother, and a Quaker minister.

Fry was a Quaker, a member of the Religious Society of Friends. Their founder, George Fox, told his followers to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." Every one: the woman in the next cell, and the woman who stole bread. Fry took it literally. She didn't start with a speech about reform. She started a small school inside the prison for the children living there with their mothers. She brought in sewing and knitting so the women could work and earn something. She gathered a group of women visitors who came back week after week. And by the usual account, she asked the prisoners themselves to agree to the rules of the new arrangement, instead of handing rules down. Then she read, plainly, out loud, from the Bible. Behind all of it sat a scene in Matthew where the king says to the righteous, in the King James Bible, "I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." The righteous ask when they ever did that, and he answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." To Fry, a prison visit was not charity from above. It was meeting Christ in a cell. Her work spread beyond Newgate. She visited women on ships carrying convicts overseas, and spoke to members of Parliament about how prisons were run. Churches still send visitors into prisons today, and the work still begins the same way: someone walks in and sits down.
screen: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YE CAME.`

segments.voice: Write a few honest lines, on paper or in your head, to someone in prison: someone you know, or a stranger you'll never meet. 929.title: Florence Nightingale
929.hook: a woman who wrote that God had called her to his service becomes the lady with the lamp
929.howItsDone: Some churches remember Florence Nightingale in their calendars, and congregations sometimes pray for nurses and health workers by name during services.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Elizabeth Fry, sitting down with the women of Newgate. Your line was I was in prison.

"Lo! in that house of misery A lady with a lamp I see." The American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote those lines about an Englishwoman working in a military hospital far from home, at Scutari, across the water from Constantinople. Soldiers lay in long rows, wounded and sick. At night, the story goes, a woman walked the wards with a lamp, checking on them one by one, and men watched for her light to pass. The poem made her a picture: soft, glowing, quiet. The real woman was tougher than the picture. Her name was Florence Nightingale.

Begin before the war. In a private note, Nightingale wrote that God had spoken to her and called her to his service. The note didn't say what the service was. She had to find out. Her family was wealthy and well connected, and nursing, in their world, was not work for a daughter like her. They resisted. She waited, read, visited hospitals when she could, and trained with a community of Lutheran deaconesses in Germany. The call didn't open a door; it kept her knocking. When she reached the war hospital, she found dirt, crowding, bad food and bad drains. She and the nurses with her scrubbed, cooked, wrote letters home for dying men, and made the night rounds Longfellow wrote about. That's the part the poem remembers. The part it forgets: Nightingale was also a woman with ledgers. She kept records, counted, and drew charts to show officials that disease, not only battle, was killing soldiers, and she argued for clean water, sewers and better hospitals long after the war. She helped found a school to train nurses. Her own religious ideas were searching and sometimes unusual, and readers still argue about them. But the shape is clear enough: a call she believed came from God, answered with a lamp at night and a pen by day. Some readers hear in it an echo of Isaiah, who hears God ask who will go, and answers, in the King James Bible: "Here am I; send me." Others honor her simply as a founder of modern nursing. Both can stand by the same bed.

Bring to mind a nurse who cared for you or someone you love: at a birth, after a fall, in a school office with an ice pack. Remember one thing they did, a blanket, a joke, a steady voice, and hold it a moment. If you pray, give thanks for them by name, or by face; if not, just let the thanks be felt.
Florence Nightingale. A woman who believed God had called her to his service, and answered with night rounds, clean water and careful records.
Your line: the lamp. A small light in a long night can be enough. Nine hundred twenty-nine days now.

930.title: George Müller's orphans
930.hook: a preacher in Bristol cares for orphans and refuses to ask anyone but God for money
930.howItsDone: Some Christian charities and missions still follow Müller's pattern of making needs known to God in prayer rather than appealing for funds, and his story is told in sermons and classes about prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Florence Nightingale, who answered her call with night rounds and careful records. Your line was the lamp.

The children are sitting at long tables. The plates are out, the cups are out. There is no breakfast in the house, and no money to buy any. That's how a story told about George Müller begins. He stands, the story says, and gives thanks for the food anyway. Then a knock at the door: a baker who couldn't sleep, and who felt he should bake bread for the orphans. Then another knock: a milkman whose cart has broken down right outside, and who would rather give the milk away than let it spoil. Whether every detail happened just so, nobody can check now. But it's the kind of story his life produced.

George Müller was a German-born preacher who settled in Bristol, in England. By his own account, he had been a wild young man, a liar and a thief, before his faith took hold. In Bristol he saw children with no parents and nowhere to go, and he opened a home for them. Then more homes. Then large orphan houses on a hill outside the city. And he set himself a strange rule: he would ask no one for money. No appeals, no debts. He would bring every need to God in prayer and nobody else. He said he wanted the work to show that God hears prayer. He leaned on lines like this one in Philippians, in the King James Bible: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Careful there means anxious. Don't be anxious; ask, and give thanks. And a psalm calls God "A father of the fatherless." Müller took that title at its word. But he didn't skip the paperwork. He kept careful records of the gifts that came in and the prayers he prayed, and he published accounts of the work. Some readers see those reports as a quiet way of letting donors know what was needed. His supporters say they were thanksgiving, a record of prayers answered. Both are honest readings. What's not in dispute is the rule itself: the children's needs were prayed for, not begged for.

Bring to mind something you need to ask someone for: help with a bill, a favor at work, an apology, a ride. Before asking, sit with the need itself, name it plainly, and notice what you're anxious about. If you pray, bring it to God first, with thanks, the way Philippians says; if you don't, hold it quietly and let the anxiety settle a little.
Müller. The Bristol preacher who opened homes for orphans and asked no one for money, bringing every need to God in prayer alone.
Your line: prayed for, not begged for. Thanks can come before the answer does. That's day nine hundred thirty.

931.title: Spurgeon
931.hook: a young Baptist preacher draws great crowds in London, and speaks honestly about his own darkness
931.howItsDone: Some pastors and churches point to Spurgeon when they speak openly about depression, and Christians in hard seasons sometimes pray Psalms 42 and 43, which ask the soul why it is cast down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Müller's orphans, and a breakfast table set with no food on it. Your line was prayed for, not begged for.

In a book of lectures for students training to be ministers, one chapter has an unexpected title: The Minister's Fainting Fits. It isn't about fainting in the pulpit. It's about the dark. Heaviness that comes for no clear reason. Weeks when the light won't come back. The lecturer was Charles Haddon Spurgeon, a Baptist preacher in London who began preaching young and drew crowds so large his congregation had to rent great halls to hold them. From the outside, he looked unshakable. He told his students the truth anyway.

Start with a terrible night. Spurgeon was preaching to a packed crowd in a rented hall when someone shouted fire. There was no fire. But people panicked and rushed for the exits, and some were crushed and died. Spurgeon was shattered, and by the accounts of people around him, that night stayed with him a long time. Over the years he also lived with painful physical sickness, and with stretches of what he plainly called depression. He would go away to rest, and come back. Then the honesty people still quote him for. He didn't tell his students that faith makes the dark impossible. He told them ministers sink low too, sometimes for no reason they can find, and that they should expect it rather than be ashamed of it. Spurgeon loved the Psalms, and Psalm 42 sounds like someone talking to himself on a bad night. In the King James Bible: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance." Notice the order. It doesn't skip the question. It asks why, out loud, and only then reaches for hope. The psalm doesn't pretend. Neither did he. And this ends a week that didn't pretend: Kierkegaard's leap, Zosima's responsibility, Newman's one step, Fry in the prison, Nightingale's lamp, Müller's empty table, and Spurgeon's honest dark. Seven lives, one of them from a novel, and none of them pretending.

Bring to mind a low stretch from your past; you don't have to relive it, just name it plainly, the way Spurgeon named his, and ask the psalm's question, why art thou cast down, without fixing anything. If it's safe to, think of one person you could tell, someday, a little of that story, and if you're in a dark time right now, let that be someone you reach out to today: a friend, a doctor, a pastor. If you pray, you can pray the psalm's line.
Spurgeon. A Baptist preacher who filled great halls in London, and told his students the truth about his own darkness.
Your line: even preachers get low. Faith never made the dark impossible, even for him. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're a famous preacher in the city, and you know the dark days well. your students are waiting for your lecture. what do you tell them?
options: nothing about it. a minister should look strong.
plainly, that ministers sink low too, and shouldn't be ashamed.
that real faith makes the dark impossible.
fork.reveal: Spurgeon gave a whole lecture on it, the minister's fainting fits. a famous voice in London told the truth.

original.note: Hebrew: my soul, from nefesh, life or self. the word in Psalm 42, why art thou cast down, O my soul.

trapdoor: what you thought: great preachers live on unshakable joy.
what it means: a preacher who filled great halls in London also went through deep darkness, and said so.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 42, a lament in which the speaker questions his own soul before turning to hope, the kind of prayer Spurgeon leaned on.
recall: Bunyan's guide who points the way

chat.says: What did Spurgeon tell young ministers about his dark days?
options: That ministers sink low too, sometimes for no clear reason, and needn't be ashamed.
That he never felt low himself, because the crowds kept his spirits high.
That he kept his dark days secret, and they should hide theirs as well.
chat.meaning: In The Minister's Fainting Fits, Spurgeon told students that ministers sink low too, sometimes for no clear reason, and should expect it, not be ashamed.

The Minister's Fainting Fits.meaning: Spurgeon's lecture on the low, dark times ministers go through
